title: SLO maturity and capacity governance blueprint
author: Ayesha Patel
body:
Summary

This blueprint defines a repeatable SLO maturity lifecycle and the governance controls that tie SLOs to capacity planning, error-budget enforcement, incident review standards, and operational tooling. The goal is to make SLO decisions auditable, predictable, and automated where possible so product and SRE teams can safely scale inference workloads without surprising customer impact or runaway cost.

Scope

- Applies to all public-facing inference services (hosted API, dedicated inference clusters, and private deployments) and core routing/ingest services that affect latency or availability.
- Excludes purely exploratory research models; those follow research onboarding guidance.

Key definitions

- SLO (Service Level Objective): Target for a user-observable metric (latency, success rate, throughput).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO (time or request-weighted). Consumed when the metric violates the SLO window.
- Headroom: Capacity margin reserved to absorb demand spikes. Expressed as percentage above expected steady-state provisioned capacity.

1) SLO maturity model (four levels)

Level 0 — Instrumented
- Minimum telemetry exists: request counts, p50/p95/p99 latency, error classification.
- No formal SLO.
- Acceptance test: Prometheus metrics available, dashboard scaffold created.

Level 1 — Defined
- At least one SLO defined with owner and target (e.g., inference-api: 99.9% success rate per 30d; realtime-warmpool: p95 < 120ms for seq_len<=128).
- Error budget computed daily and surfaced to teams.
- Acceptance test: SLO document page and daily error-budget email subscription.

Level 2 — Operationalized
- Automated alerts triggered on burn-rate thresholds and capacity signals.
- Canonical rollout and rollback gates require SLO checks before production rollouts.
- Acceptance test: Canary runs fail fast if projected burn > 2x baseline.

Level 3 — Stewarded
- SLO changes require cross-team approval and capacity reservation. Error-budget remediation runbooks are automated and invoked.
- Periodic maturity reviews (quarterly).
- Acceptance test: Postmortem evidence links SLO changes and capacity provisioning decisions.

2) Recommended SLO types and examples

- Availability / Success rate (user-visible errors): 99.9% per 30d for hosted-text-gen; non-critical internal endpoints may target 99.5%.
- Latency quantile (tail): p95 and p99 for typical request classes. Example: embed-service p95 < 250ms under normal load.
- Freshness / correctness (for caching-backed endpoints): staleness window < 2 minutes.

Example SLO definition (plain text)
- service: inference-api
- objective: 99.9% successful responses (HTTP 2xx) over 30d, weighted by token_count
- measurement: PromQL: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api",status=~"2.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api"}[30d]))
- owner: inference-service-product@redwood.com

3) Error budget policy and escalation matrix

We use a dual-trigger model: a burn-rate (short window) and remaining budget (long window). Automated actions are tiered and time-bounded.

- Green (<= 25% budget used in 30d): Normal operations.
- Watch (25% - 50%): Product and SRE notified; prepare mitigations; defer low-priority releases.
- Action (50% - 75%): Hold new feature rollouts for this service; SRE kicks off the Remediation Run (see Runbooks).
- Guardrail (75% - 100%): Apply capacity hedges (increase pool by configured reserve), enable graceful degradation modes (lower-quality model fallback), and notify GTM.
- Breach (>100%): Follow Incident Response playbook and trigger post-incident review; may require credits/notifications per contract.

Burn-rate thresholds are computed over a 1h and 24h window and compared against expected baseline burn-rate. If 1h burn-rate > 4x baseline OR 24h burn-rate > 2x baseline, escalate one tier immediately.

4) Capacity planning and headroom formulas

Principles
- Capacity is provisioned against a 95th percentile demand forecast plus a headroom buffer for burst absorption.
- Separate models for short-tail latency-sensitive requests vs. long-running/embedding workloads.
- Multi-tenant fairness enforced via token-priority lanes and soft-eviction explained below.

Simple headroom formula (example)
- steady_request_rate = predicted RPS at 95th percentile (30d window)
- worker_capacity = avg_tokens_per_second_per_gpu * gpu_count
- required_gpus = ceil((steady_request_rate * avg_tokens_per_request) / (worker_capacity * (1 - safety_buffer)))
- safety_buffer default = 0.18 (18% headroom) for inference-api; critical services default = 0.25.

Capacity reservation policy
- Team requests for guaranteed capacity (Dedicated) must provide: 30d traffic fingerprint, max-concurrency, 99th percentile token-rate, planned rollout dates.
- On approval, the capacity owner creates a capacity ticket with tags: service, start_date, end_date, reserved_gpus, owner.

5) Multi-tenant throttling and eviction rules

- Priority lanes: realtime > interactive > batch. Each lane has a target minimum capacity slice.
- Soft preemption: when contention hits threshold, batch requests are delayed (queue TTL=60s) then dropped with structured error code X-RateLimit-Recoverable.
- Hard eviction: only applied after 3 progressive soft preemption cycles or when SLO breach is imminent; leadership approval required for forced eviction of dedicated tenants.

6) Operational tooling and dashboards (minimum set)

Dashboards (must exist for Level 1+)
- SLO summary panel: per-service error budget remaining, burn-rate (1h/24h), owner contact.
- Capacity panel: provisioned GPUs, utilization heatmap, warm-pool occupancy, token throughput by model family.
- Incident correlation: traces linked to SLO breaches and capacity events.

Alerts and automation
- Alert: SLO-watch (remaining budget <50% and 24h burn_rate > 1.5x) — notify #sre-slo and create ticket in SLO-Remediation queue.
- Alert: Capacity-pressure (GPU utilization > 85% for 10m and p95 latency increase > 20%) — trigger autoscale and send runbook button to oncall.
- Automation: Runbook buttons exposed in PagerDuty incident and Slack channel to execute: scale-up pool, enable fallback-model-route, and annotate SLO ticket.

PromQL examples included as text (copyable)
- error_budget_remaining: (1 - (sum(increase(slo_violations_total{service=~".*"}[30d])) / sum(increase(requests_total{service=~".*"}[30d])))) * 100
- gpu_utilization_pct: 100 * (sum(gpu_secs_active) / sum(gpu_secs_allocated))

7) Runbook excerpts (links to canonical runbooks are required; excerpts below illustrate governance flow)

Remediation run (triggered at Action tier)
1. Triage: oncall captures timeline and annotates SLO ticket with initial hypothesis and recent deploys. (10m)
2. Immediate mitigations (15m): toggle heavier batching off, reduce quantization aggressiveness if latency increases are from CPU-side ops, enable fallback model if available.
3. Capacity hedge (30m): if automation approves, add +20% warm-pool capacity for 2 hours.
4. Monitor: confirm error-budget slope reduces; if not, escalate to Incident Response.

Throttle and eviction run (for multi-tenant exhaustion)
1. Identify top 5 tenants by token consumption in last 15m.
2. Apply per-tenant soft-throttle (reduce concurrency, increase queue TTL penalty).
3. If soft-throttle ineffective after 20m and SLOs still degrading, move to eviction with product and legal notification.

8) Incident review standards (evidence & remediation)

Required artifacts for any post-incident SLO breach:
- Chronological timeline with timestamps and who performed actions.
- Telemetry snapshot: SLO panels, traces, top N token consumers, autoscaler events.
- Deploy state and config diff for the 2 hours before breach.
- Decision log documenting remediation and capacity actions taken.

RCA expectations
- Root cause must be expressed as causal chain (change -> catalyst -> manifestation -> impact) and tied to a concrete follow-up (owner + due date).
- If capacity choices contributed, include a capacity action (reserve/top-up/guardrail) in the follow-up.

9) Governance cadence and roles

- Weekly SLO digest (automated) — owners receive a 1-pager of SLO trends and top regressions.
- Quarterly SLO review board — participants: SRE lead, product steward, infra planner, and a representative from customer success for enterprise-impact SLOs.
- Role matrix (short):
  - SLO owner: defines objective, acceptance tests, and runbook edits (typically product+service team).
  - Capacity owner: approves reservations and runs provisioning (infra/SRE).
  - Steward (SRE): audits SLO maturity and triggers governance steps.

10) Sample rollout gating checklist (must be completed before major production rollout)

- Canary run for 48 hours with shadow traffic at 10% and SLO projection check: projected additional burn < 10% of budget.
- Load tests that include cold-start and KV-cache-warm scenarios with p95 latency below target.
- Capacity ticket filed (if projected steady-state increase > 5% of cluster capacity).
- Observability: dashboards and alerts defined and validated (screenshot attached to ticket).

Appendix: quick commands and contacts

- To compute projected error budget remaining (example Prometheus query snippet): refer to the PromQL examples above.
- SRE oncall rotation: #sre-oncall (Slack), pager: PD SRE rota.
- Capacity requests: create ticket with label capacity-request and tag infra-capacity@redwood.com.

Ownership and maintenance

- Document owner: Ayesha Patel (SRE platform). Quarterly review scheduled.
- Change process: edits require at least one SRE reviewer and one product reviewer listed in the reviewers section.

Related artifacts

- See product-specific rollout checklists and runbook pages linked in the related_pages field.

This blueprint is intended to be pragmatic: focus on measurable SLOs, short feedback loops between error budget and capacity actions, and tight evidence requirements for post-incident decisions.
